paragraphs: Before the night of the fourteenth [of Nisan], one must clean all the rooms and houses in the courtyard, and the woman of the house should also examine well the pockets of all the clothing, lest chametz was placed in them, and even where there is only a doubt she must check and look. Then, at the start of the night of the fourteenth, one checks for chametz by candlelight right after the stars come out, immediately; and one should wash his hands before reciting the blessing over the search (bedikah), as mentioned by the Acharonim, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: Before the night of the 14th of Nisan, all the rooms and houses in the courtyard are cleaned, and the woman also checks the pockets of the clothing well lest chametz was placed in them, and even where there is only a doubt one must check. At the start of the night of the 14th, immediately after the stars come out, one checks for chametz by candlelight. One washes hands before the blessing over the search.
takeaways: The house is cleaned and clothing pockets checked before the night of the 14th
The search takes place immediately after the stars come out, by candlelight, after washing hands

paragraphs: One must search by the light of a single wax candle, and should not bring two candles that are joined or stuck together, which is considered a torch (avukah); one does not search by torchlight. The candles that are not used for the search were given the mnemonic “Chashash-a,” which stands for chelev (tallow), shemen (oil), shuman (fat), avukah (torch) – see “Moed LeChol Chai.” The candles that currently come to our city from the cities of Europe are made of tallow, and one does not light them [for the search].

clarification.explanation: One searches by the light of a single wax candle, and should not use two candles stuck together which are like a torch, since one does not search by torchlight. A mnemonic for candles not used for the search: Chashash-a (tallow, oil, fat, torch). The candles that arrive in the city from Europe are made of tallow and should not be lit for the search.
takeaways: Search by the light of a single wax candle, not a torch and not a tallow candle

paragraphs: One must search in the cracks and crevices and in every place where chametz is brought in, and should not cut the search short even though it is a great burden, since the walls of the house are built of small stones without plaster, for this mitzvah is very great, and the reward is according to the exertion. He should search in the recessed places built into the walls, called in Arabic “ruwazin” (window ledges and wall protrusions), and the like. And if he forgot or was prevented and did not search at night, he should search during the day immediately after the morning prayer, and the search should be by candlelight; only in a well-lit veranda is a candle not necessary.

clarification.explanation: One searches in holes and cracks and every place where chametz is usually brought, and should not be lazy even though the effort is great, for this is a great mitzvah and the reward matches the exertion. One also searches in recesses and protrusions in the walls. One who forgot or was prevented and did not search at night should search during the day immediately after Shacharit by candlelight, and only in a very well-lit place is a candle unnecessary.
takeaways: Search every place where chametz is brought in, even with effort
Forgot at night - search during the day after Shacharit by candlelight

paragraphs: One should not begin any work, nor eat, until he has searched; but a mere taste of fruit, or less than the volume of an egg of bread, is permitted before the search. And even one who has a fixed time for study should not study until he has searched.

clarification.explanation: One should not begin any work and should not eat until searching. It is permitted to taste a little fruit, or less than an egg's volume of bread, before the search. Also one who has a fixed time for study should not study until he has searched.
takeaways: Work, eating, or study is not begun until the search is finished

paragraphs: Before the search he should recite the blessing “…Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the removal of chametz,” since the search serves the removal. And even though this mitzvah recurs from time to time, one does not recite Shehecheyanu over it. However, the Acharonim wrote that if he happens to have a new garment or a new fruit, he should recite Shehecheyanu [over that] and intend to also exempt this mitzvah. And if he forgot and did not recite the blessing over the removal of chametz, he may recite it as long as he has not finished the search. And if the members of the household are searching with him, he alone recites the blessing, and he and they should intend to fulfill their obligation; and he should not speak between the blessing and the start of the search – and if he spoke about something unrelated to the search, he must repeat the blessing. It is good that he not speak of other matters until he finishes the entire search. He should first put away the chametz that he has for his own eating, and cover it with a vessel.

clarification.explanation: Before the search one recites the blessing “concerning the removal of chametz,” since the search serves the purpose of removal, and one does not recite Shehecheyanu over it. If he happens to have a new garment or fruit he should recite Shehecheyanu and intend to also exempt this mitzvah. If he forgot to recite the blessing, he can recite it as long as he has not finished; and if the household members search with him, he alone recites the blessing and all intend to fulfill their obligation. One should not speak between the blessing and the start of the search, and if he spoke about something unrelated to the search he must repeat the blessing. He should first put away the chametz he leaves for his own eating and cover it with a vessel.
takeaways: One recites the blessing “concerning the removal of chametz” before the search
One must not speak between the blessing and the start of the search

paragraphs: The custom is that the one searching carries a bowl containing a piece of bread and a knife, in order to poke with it into holes and cracks; and some have the custom of placing ten pieces of chametz in the corners of the house before the search, so that the searcher will find them and remove them. Here in our city of Baghdad the custom is to place a little salt in the aforementioned bowl, the reason being that Satan and his cohort are very envious of the mitzvah of searching for chametz, and therefore one carries salt along with the searcher to repel the accusers and prosecutors, in the manner of what was said about placing salt on the table. And there is another reason [given], that this is done as a good omen, that we merit many years to search each and every year, for salt is a sign of endurance, as it is written, “a covenant of salt” (Numbers 18:19), which is something that endures.

clarification.explanation: The custom is to carry along with the searcher a bowl with a piece of bread and a knife to poke into holes and cracks, and some place ten pieces of chametz in the corners of the house before the search so that the searcher will find and remove them. In Baghdad the custom is to place a little salt in the bowl, to repel the prosecutors who are envious of this mitzvah, and also as a good omen and sign of endurance like “a covenant of salt,” that we may merit to search for many years.
takeaways: Carrying a bowl with bread and a knife; the custom of placing ten pieces [of chametz]
In Baghdad a bit of salt is added as a good omen

paragraphs: Immediately after the search at night, one nullifies the chametz and recites “Kol chamira… d’la chazitei… l’vatel v’lehevei k’afra d’ar’a” (“All leaven… that I have not seen… shall be nullified and be as the dust of the earth”). One must understand that the word “chamira” is a term that includes both chametz and se'or (leaven). One must also understand that the nullification consists of rendering it ownerless (hefker), with no rights over it remaining. And he should recite the nullification three times, as written in “Machazik Berachah.”

clarification.explanation: Immediately after the nighttime search one nullifies the chametz, saying “Kol chamira… d’la chazitei… l’vatel v’lehevei k’afra d’ar’a.” One must understand that the word “chamira” includes both chametz and se'or, and that the nullification renders the chametz ownerless, with no remaining rights over it. The nullification is recited three times.
takeaways: The chametz is nullified immediately after the search, and one understands the meaning of the words
The nullification is recited three times

paragraphs: Chametz is forbidden to eat on the fourteenth day from the fourth hour onward, but it is permitted for benefit even into the fifth hour; these are seasonal (temporal) hours, and we count them from dawn. After eating it, he should clean his teeth with a thin piece of wood, inserting it into the gaps and cracks between the teeth so that no chametz remains stuck there, and after cleaning he should wash and rinse his mouth well with water and rub his teeth well with his finger, for on Passover chametz is forbidden even in the smallest amount. There is a story about a man who was very careful in guarding the matzah during kneading and baking and in all the laws of Pesach; on the night of Pesach, after he fell asleep, he dreamed that a man said to him, “Woe to him who ate a bit of chametz.” He awoke and was greatly distressed and wept bitterly, and then fell back asleep in the midst of his weeping, and dreamed again, and behold a man spoke with him and said, “This chametz that you ate is a small crumb that remained between your teeth from a meal you ate on the morning of the eve of Pesach, and while you were eating and chewing the matzah at night, that crumb came loose from between your teeth and stuck to the matzah, and you ate it together with the matzah.” Therefore, a person must take this matter greatly to heart, to be careful to clean his teeth well.

clarification.explanation: Chametz is forbidden to eat on the 14th from the start of the fifth hour (temporal hours from dawn), and it is permitted for benefit even in the fifth hour. After eating, one cleans the teeth well with a thin piece of wood and washes the mouth, since on Pesach chametz is forbidden even in the tiniest amount. A story is brought of a man who dreamed that he had eaten chametz from a crumb that remained between his teeth from before Pesach and became mixed into the matzah - to teach us how careful one must be to clean the teeth well.
takeaways: Chametz is forbidden to eat from the fifth hour of the 14th
Clean well between the teeth, since chametz is forbidden even in the tiniest amount

paragraphs: One who has chametz in his store and cannot remove it from the store, and must sell it to a non-Jew while it is still in the store, should be careful to sell it in accordance with the law: he should receive money from the non-Jew and explicitly tell him that he is selling him all such-and-such chametz that he has in his store, and that he is also selling him all the vessels in which the chametz is placed – so that they not be regarded as the seller’s own vessels remaining in the buyer’s domain, which he would not have acquired. He should hand him all the keys to the store and explicitly tell him that he is handing him the keys so that he may enter the store whenever he wishes and do with the chametz inside as he pleases, like a person doing as he wishes with his own property, with no one in the world to protest. However, it is better still not to do this by way of a sale but by way of a gift – that he give the chametz and the vessels in which it is placed as a complete and perfect gift to the non-Jew, and hand him the keys to the store so that the non-Jew may go and do with the chametz as he pleases – because the way of a gift is more proper, since sales are not always done correctly. All this he should do in the morning immediately after Shacharit, so that he not forget due to being preoccupied. And even though this non-Jew returns everything to him after Pesach and derives no benefit at all, there is nothing wrong with this, since in truth the non-Jew acquired all of it according to the law. And those who have sweets containing flour should not keep them in the house, but should sell them to a non-Jew or give them to him as a complete gift, even though the non-Jew returns them after Pesach. Likewise those who have grain called “burghul” (parched and ground wheat), and a drink called “beer,” must sell it to a non-Jew or give it to him as a complete gift, and he should take it to his own house. And if they forgot and did not sell them or give them as a gift to a non-Jew before Pesach, and Pesach passed over them, they are forbidden for benefit after Pesach. However, sugar that comes from the cities of India, and likewise “qand” (translucent blocks of sugar) coming from the cities of Europe, and likewise a sweet called “nabat” (blocks of sugar shaped like a bottle) – it is permitted to keep them in the house during Pesach, and one only does not eat from them during Pesach. And one who has chametz on a ship or in a caravan should sell it to a non-Jew with money and a document, and should come to the teacher to learn from him the text of the document, how it is [written].

clarification.explanation: One who has chametz in his store and cannot remove it should sell it to a non-Jew while it is still in the store: he should receive money from him, explicitly state that he is selling him all the chametz and the vessels containing it, and hand him all the keys so he may enter and do with the chametz as he wishes. It is preferable to do this by way of a complete gift rather than a sale. He should do this in the morning right after Shacharit lest he forget, and even though the non-Jew returns everything after Pesach - the acquisition is valid. Also sweets containing flour, burghul, and beer - he should sell or give them to the non-Jew, and if he forgot and Pesach passed over them, they are forbidden for benefit; but sugar from India and blocks of sugar from Europe are permitted to be kept in the house, only one does not eat from them during Pesach. And one who has chametz on a ship or in a caravan should sell it to a non-Jew with money and a document, and should come to his teacher to learn the text of the document.
takeaways: Chametz in a store is sold to a non-Jew as a complete gift, with the keys handed over
Chametz that Pesach passed over is forbidden for benefit; raw sugar is permitted to be kept

paragraphs: After he finishes eating on the fourteenth day, he himself, in person, should burn the remaining chametz, for there is greater merit in doing the mitzvah oneself than through a messenger. But it is forbidden to throw the chametz into the public domain because of the degradation involved, and it also constitutes a desecration of God’s name in the eyes of the non-Jews. The custom is to burn it in the courtyard using a willow branch from Hoshana Rabbah – see “Chayim LeRosh,” page 12. After burning it, he should nullify it immediately and say “d’chazitei ud’la chazitei…” (“that I have seen and that I have not seen…”), and recite the nullification three times, and he should not nullify it before the burning, in order to fulfill the mitzvah of burning his own chametz. And if he borrowed a loaf [of bread] before Pesach, it is best to return it before Pesach; and if he did not return it beforehand, he should return it after Pesach, and there is no concern in this; but if he does not return it, this constitutes theft.

clarification.explanation: After finishing eating on the 14th, he himself burns the remaining chametz, since there is more merit in doing it himself than through a messenger, and it is forbidden to throw chametz into the public domain because of the degradation and desecration of God's name. The custom is to burn it in the courtyard with a willow branch from Hoshana Rabbah. After the burning he nullifies it immediately, saying “d'chazitei ud'la chazitei” three times, and not before the burning, so as to fulfill the mitzvah of burning his own chametz. One who borrowed a loaf before Pesach should preferably return it before Pesach, and if not - afterward.
takeaways: He burns the chametz himself, and it is forbidden to throw it into the public domain
He nullifies it after the burning, three times

paragraphs: One who wears a new shirt made of the kind of fabric containing “chametz nukesha” called in Arabic “nasha” (wheat starch), must launder it very thoroughly before Pesach – soaking it in water before washing so that he can remove this “nasha” from it by laundering – and [only then] wear it during the festival. For if this “nasha” remains in it, it is likely that this “nasha” will come into his mouth during the festival, at a time when chametz is forbidden in the smallest amount, since people’s way is, such as when tying their trousers in the outhouse, to hold the shirt in their teeth, and also sometimes to wipe their mouth and teeth with their shirt. Likewise one should be careful to launder before the festival new handkerchiefs coming from the cities of Europe, since these too contain the “chametz nukesha” called “nasha”; and likewise one should launder the tablecloth spread on the table on which one eats, which contains “nasha,” and likewise a cloth spread on the beds when people sit on them at their meal at the table, in case a piece of moist bread or moist fruit falls on it and picks up some of the aforementioned “nasha” and one then tastes it in one’s mouth, and the like.

clarification.explanation: One who wears a new shirt of fabric containing hard chametz (wheat starch called “nasha”) must launder it very well before Pesach and soak it in water beforehand to remove the starch - for if it remains, it may reach his mouth during the festival when chametz is forbidden even in the smallest amount, since people are in the habit of holding the shirt in their teeth or wiping their mouth with it. Likewise one should launder new handkerchiefs from Europe, tablecloths, and bedspreads used at meals, which also contain this starch.
takeaways: New garments containing wheat starch are laundered and soaked before Pesach
Care is taken with handkerchiefs and tablecloths that might touch food

paragraphs: One should not use chametz vessels on Pesach without kashering, and the kashering [required] depends on the vessel’s use: if chametz was used in it with liquid [cooked] in boiling water, its kashering is by hag’alah (immersion) in boiling water. He should not put the vessel into the water unless it is actually boiling, and if it has stopped boiling, he should light more fire and bring the water back to a boil, and only then perform the hag’alah in it. It is good to let the vessel remain a little while in the boiling water, enough for the boiling water to penetrate the thickness of the vessel and for the absorbed matter to be expelled outward, as mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch of our teacher Rabbeinu Zalman, of blessed memory – but specifically when it is brief should one let it remain; one should not let it remain long. Before the hag’alah, he should scour it well and remove all rust from it, and if there are pits from which the rust cannot be cleaned, libun (fire-purging) is required at the location of the pits. The handles of the vessels also require hag’alah, and one should be careful to perform the hag’alah before the fifth hour, so as not to need several additional conditions; and even one who performs hag’alah before the fifth hour should be careful that the vessels not be “vessels of the day” [i.e., used within the past 24 hours], since one should not pass a forbidden vessel [through kashering] unless it is not “of the day” – for during the rest of the year one does not kasher a forbidden vessel unless it is not “of the day.” One performing hag’alah with tongs should turn the vessel over, and the lid of a bowl also requires hag’alah. And it is written in “Sha’ar Ta’amei HaMitzvot,” Parashat Eikev, a warning from our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory: One should be careful not to whiten copper vessels with melted tin, as is the common practice, [before using them] for matzah, until they have first been given hag’alah – for this melted tin becomes a coating over the copper and prevents the expulsion of the chametz from within it if it is later given hag’alah; and libun on the tin itself does not help, since the Sages set a measure for libun that sparks must fly off from it, and the libun of the tin coating will not reach the measure of sparks flying off. Therefore it is better to first perform hag’alah to expel the chametz, and afterward have the non-Jew whiten it with tin in his presence; and one should be careful not to then extinguish the vessel in the water in front of the craftsman with which he extinguishes chametz vessels – until here his words, to be examined there. And here in our cities, may they be protected, this has not been the practice; rather, vessels that are used with hot liquids throughout the year are first whitened with tin, and afterward given hag’alah for use on Pesach, and we do not protest against them – since here in our city it is not the practice to cook actual chametz in these vessels during the rest of the year, such as a dish containing bread or flour; only in a frying pan is it the practice to fry dough made of flour, and even so this is not its main use. Therefore we do not protest against those who act according to the aforementioned warning of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory – though certainly a God-fearing person should be careful about this, and likewise regarding a vessel that became forbidden due to meat and milk, and likewise other forbidden vessels that one wishes to whiten with tin and give hag’alah – every person should be careful in this, to give hag’alah first and afterward whiten with tin, as per the aforementioned warning of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: One must not use chametz vessels on Pesach without kashering, and the kashering depends on the vessel's use: a vessel in which chametz was cooked in boiling liquid is kashered by hag'alah in actually boiling water. One must clean it well and remove rust before the hag'alah, and where there are pits that cannot be cleaned of rust, libun is required there. Handles and lids also require hag'alah, [performed] before the fifth hour and while the vessels are not “of the day.” The Ari, of blessed memory, further warned not to whiten copper vessels with tin before hag'alah, since the tin forms a barrier preventing the expulsion of the chametz - rather one should first give hag'alah and only afterward have it whitened with tin. The Ben Ish Chai notes that in Baghdad the practice was not to be exacting about this order, but rather to whiten with tin first and only afterward perform hag'alah, and we do not protest against those who follow this practice; but a God-fearing person should be careful to follow the words of the Ari, of blessed memory - to give hag'alah first and whiten afterward - and the same law applies to any forbidden vessel, such as one forbidden due to meat and milk, that one wishes to whiten with tin.
takeaways: Chametz vessels are kashered according to their use; those used with boiling liquid - by hag'alah
Hag'alah is done before the fifth hour, after cleaning off rust

Hag'alah should be done first, and only afterward should the vessel be whitened with tin, per the words of the Ari, of blessed memory - even though in Baghdad the practice was in fact to be lenient and not particular about this

paragraphs: The custom is to rinse the vessels in cold water after hag’alah, so that the vessel not absorb the residue of the boiling water on its surface, since the vessel’s expelled matter has mixed into the boiling water; and even though it has become nullified in sixty [parts], nevertheless the custom is, as a preferred practice, to remove this by rinsing in cold water, as mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman, of blessed memory; and the “Levush” wrote another reason for this.

clarification.explanation: The custom is to rinse the vessels in cold water after hag'alah, so that the vessel not absorb the residue in the boiling water into which the chametz expelled by the vessel became mixed. And even though that expelled matter has become nullified in sixty parts, nonetheless the preferred practice is to remove this by rinsing in cold water.
takeaways: Rinse in cold water immediately after hag'alah

paragraphs: Vessels that were used with fire in a dry manner, such as spits and grates called in Arabic “sajat” (metal grates and spits for roasting), that had chametz used in them, require libun to kasher them for Pesach, and hag’alah does not help for them. A frying pan used for frying is sufficient with hag’alah, but our teacher Rabbi Moshe, of blessed memory, wrote that it requires libun, and one who is stringent to give it libun will be blessed; however, it does not require a great libun such that sparks fly off from it, but rather a libun sufficient that straw would be burned upon it from the outside. And earthenware vessels, even those coated with what is called “firfuri” (lead glazing), in which a boiling liquid [poured] from a second vessel was used – no kashering at all will help them; rather, one should clean them well and put them away in a closed place, so that he not mistakenly use them on Pesach. And bowls that are metal vessels coated with fused glass should not be given hag’alah. And all glass vessels that were used with cold [liquid], even if a beverage made from barley called “beer” was used in them, are permitted to be used on Pesach by way of “eiruy” – he fills them with water and lets them stand for twenty-four hours, and after twenty-four hours he pours them out and refills them with fresh water, letting them stand another twenty-four hours, and pours them out and refills them again with fresh water for another twenty-four hours – and thereby they are permitted to be used on Pesach, since their original absorption was with a cold [liquid].

clarification.explanation: Vessels used with fire in a dry manner, such as spits and roasting grates that had chametz in them, require libun to kasher them, and hag'alah does not help for them. A frying pan used for frying is sufficient with hag'alah, though some are stringent to give it libun as well. Earthenware vessels, even coated ones, that were used with boiling liquid have no kashering available; rather, one should clean and put them away in a closed place lest he mistakenly use them. Glass vessels used with cold liquid (even beer) are permitted on Pesach by way of “eiruy” - filling them with water three times, twenty-four hours each time, since their absorption was originally with a cold liquid.
takeaways: Spits and roasting grates - libun; a frying pan - hag'alah
Earthenware vessels have no kashering available; glass vessels - filling with water three times

paragraphs: During the rest of the year, if one buys an old metal vessel from a non-Jew, he must first give it hag’alah, and afterward immerse it [in a mikveh], reciting the blessing “concerning the immersion of a vessel” – and if there are two or more vessels, he recites “concerning the immersion of vessels” – such is the custom here in our city, may it be protected; and not like the one who says one recites “concerning the immersion of vessels” even when immersing a single vessel. And vessels used to hold wine or beer for storage, called in Arabic “qararib” (large glass containers), have the same law as metal vessels. And if he bought new ones, he immerses them and recites the blessing, following the opinion of Rabbi “Beit David,” of blessed memory, and not like Rabbi “Mateh Yehudah,” of blessed memory – so agreed the crown of our heads, my grandfather, the Gaon Rabbeinu Moshe Chaim, of blessed memory, and so was the practice established here in our city of Baghdad from ancient years, and so would he expound in public every Shabbat HaGadol, and so would the crown of our heads, my father, of blessed memory, expound every Shabbat HaGadol, and so I, the servant, expound every Shabbat HaGadol, with the help of God, blessed be He; thus the custom in this matter is found to be clear and firmly established, and there is no doubtful concern here regarding blessings, to be lenient.

clarification.explanation: During the rest of the year, one who buys an old metal vessel from a non-Jew must first give it hag'alah and then immerse it in a mikveh, reciting “concerning the immersion of a vessel” - or “vessels” if there are two or more - such is the custom here in our city. Large glass containers used to store wine or beer have the same law as metal vessels. If he bought new ones, he immerses them and recites the blessing, and this is the clear, long-established custom in Baghdad, with no doubtful concern regarding the blessings.
takeaways: A metal vessel from a non-Jew - give hag'alah and then immerse with a blessing
Glass storage vessels have the same law as metal vessels for immersion

paragraphs: One should knead only with “our water” (mayim shelanu – rested water), drawn close to twilight or during twilight itself. The Gaon Rabbi Chaim Palagi, of blessed memory, wrote in “Chayim LeRosh”: the limited time for drawing is ten minutes before the call to the “Maghreb” (evening prayer); such that once twelve hours have been completed in full and the Maghreb has been called, he should then immediately stop drawing any more – see there. And it is forbidden as a preferred practice to draw [water] for “matzat mitzvah” through a non-Jew; and one should be careful to wash his hands before drawing, and should say aloud, “Behold, I am drawing water for the sake of matzat mitzvah.”

clarification.explanation: One should knead matzot only with “our water” (rested water), drawn close to sunset or during twilight. The time for drawing is about ten minutes before the call to evening prayer, and once twelve hours have fully passed and the call to prayer has sounded, one must stop drawing. It is forbidden as a preferred practice to draw water for matzat mitzvah through a non-Jew, and one washes hands before drawing and says, “Behold, I am drawing water for the sake of matzat mitzvah.”
takeaways: “Our water” is drawn close to sunset, not through a non-Jew
Hands are washed and a declaration is made that the drawing is for the sake of matzat mitzvah

paragraphs: It is good that a menstruating woman (niddah) not touch the water drawn for matzat mitzvah, as written in “Chayim LeRosh.” One should be careful to cover the mouth of the jug well so that nothing falls into it. And if he leaves them overnight on the roof, he should be careful to bring them down before sunrise, lest he forget them and the sun rise upon them, or lest it be a cloudy day where the whole day turns out sunny [after being expected cloudy]. And if he has a veranda, it is good to leave them there overnight.

clarification.explanation: It is good that a niddah not touch the water drawn for matzat mitzvah. One should cover the mouth of the jug well so that nothing falls in. If the water is left overnight on the roof, one should bring it down before sunrise lest he forget and the sun shine on it, or the day turn out sunny [despite appearing cloudy]. If he has a veranda, it is good to leave the water there at night.
takeaways: The water is covered and brought down from the roof before sunrise

paragraphs: Both for matzat mitzvah and for other matzot, one must be careful not to knead before dawn, since one must wait on the water for the duration of at least one full night before kneading with it. And on the eve of Pesach, if one is forced to knead before dawn due to large quantities, he must draw the water during twilight of the night of the thirteenth; but if he drew it during twilight of the night of the fourteenth, he may not knead with this water before dawn, since at least one full night is required – even though some are particular to require twelve hours from the time of drawing. In a case of pressing need and great necessity, one may rely on those who hold that one night suffices, even if it does not contain twelve hours. And one must warn, when taking water out of the barrel to give for kneading, not to put his hands into the water, since the hands are warm and warm the dough, as our teacher Rabbeinu Zalman, of blessed memory, wrote in the Shulchan Aruch. Also, one must be careful not to knead flour after grinding until twenty-four hours have passed over it, since grinding heats it up.

clarification.explanation: For both matzat mitzvah and other matzot, one must not knead before dawn, since the water must rest a full night beforehand. On the eve of Pesach, if forced to knead before dawn due to large quantities, the water must be drawn during twilight of the night of the thirteenth. As a preferred practice some require a full twelve hours from the time of drawing until kneading, but in a case of pressing and great need one may rely on those who hold that one night suffices, even without twelve hours. One must not put his hands into the water, since the hands are warm and heat the dough; and one must not knead flour until twenty-four hours have passed since grinding, since grinding heats it.
takeaways: Kneading is done only after the water has rested a full night
As a preferred practice a full twelve hours from the time of drawing is required, but in pressing need one may rely on one night alone being sufficient
Hands are not put into the water; flour is not kneaded within twenty-four hours of grinding

paragraphs: One should not knead a batch of dough for Pesach larger than 520 dirhams, and it is better to knead it at less than 520. The measure of dough obligated in challah is flour weighing seven hundred seventy-seven dirhams, since this comes out to 43 and one-fifth eggs’ worth, at a weight of 18 dirhams per egg, as mentioned by the halachic authorities – see “Chayim LeRosh,” page 110. Since we are careful that the dough kneaded for Pesach not reach the measure obligated in challah, it is therefore good to place all the matzot after baking into a single basket, so that the basket combines them for the purpose of challah, and then he separates challah and recites the blessing. And if he has no basket or single container to combine them, he should place the matzot in one place and spread a cloth over them so that none of the matzot are exposed at all, and then separate challah. The blessing for challah is “…Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to separate challah, terumah.” And even though there is one who wrote that the text is “terumah, challah,” the custom here in our city is to say the blessing as “challah, terumah,” and so would the crown of our heads, my grandfather, of blessed memory, and the crown of our heads, my father, of blessed memory, expound in public every Shabbat HaGadol, and I have heard that this is likewise the custom in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and established speedily.

clarification.explanation: One should not knead a batch for Pesach larger than 520 dirhams, and it is better to keep it below that, so that it does not reach the measure obligated in challah (777 dirhams of flour). Since we are careful that the dough not reach the measure for challah, it is good to place all the matzot after baking into one basket, which combines them for challah, and then separate and bless. If there is no basket, one places them together and spreads a cloth over them so none are exposed, and separates. The text of the blessing in Baghdad is “to separate challah, terumah.”
takeaways: A batch smaller than 520 dirhams so it does not become obligated in challah
The matzot are combined in a basket or under a cloth and challah is separated with a blessing

paragraphs: If one forgot and did not separate challah before Yom Tov, and remembered on Yom Tov itself, challah is not separated on Yom Tov, as written in the Shulchan Aruch, siman 506. What should he do? He should eat without [separating] challah, and set aside one matzah until the end of Yom Tov and separate challah from that matzah, since for challah [taken] outside the Land [of Israel] one may eat first and separate afterward. And even though there are those who say that we do not apply “eat first and separate afterward” outside the Land except specifically where the dough already had the measure obligating challah while it was still dough – but if the dough did not have the measure for challah, and only afterward [several batches] were combined in one vessel and became obligated in challah, then setting aside one matzah to separate challah from it at the end of Yom Tov would not help; rather, one must set aside a little from each and every matzah in order to tithe from that which is adjoining [“min hamukaf”] – nevertheless, I have concluded in my small book “Mikabtzi’el” that the primary [ruling] follows the opinion of those who disagree, who hold that even in such a case, where there was no [challah] measure in the dough originally, but only after baking he placed them in a vessel to combine them, it is nonetheless effective to eat from them before separating challah, and only afterward set aside one matzah and separate challah from it. Therefore, if one forgot and did not separate before Yom Tov, he may rely on this position to eat and separate afterward from one matzah – see the Shulchan Aruch of our teacher Rabbeinu Zalman, of blessed memory, Hilchot Pesach, siman 457, se’ifim 10 and 11, to be examined there.

clarification.explanation: If one forgot to separate challah before Yom Tov and remembered on the day itself - challah is not separated on Yom Tov. What should he do? He should eat without challah, set aside one matzah until the end of Yom Tov, and separate challah from it, since [for] challah outside the Land one eats first and separates afterward. And although there are those who disagree when the dough did not have the measure for challah in itself but only after being combined afterward in a vessel, here he ruled to rely on the lenient opinion, to eat and separate afterward from one matzah.
takeaways: Forgot to separate challah - one eats, sets aside a matzah, and separates at the end of Yom Tov

paragraphs: After he recites the blessing and separates, he should say aloud, “This is challah,” in order to give it that designation verbally after the blessing. And even though there are many who hold that one need not give it a verbal designation, nevertheless, since there are eminent authorities who hold this way, what loss is there in saying these three words, so as to act in accordance with everyone’s opinion? So have I concluded, with God’s help, in a responsum in my holy book “Rav Pe’alim.”

clarification.explanation: After reciting the blessing and separating, one says aloud “This is challah,” to give it a verbal designation after the blessing. And although many hold that no verbal designation is required, since there are eminent authorities who hold that it is, there is no loss in saying these three words, so as to satisfy all opinions.
takeaways: One says “This is challah” after the separation, so as to satisfy all opinions

paragraphs: The Rosh, of blessed memory, would exert himself to make matzat mitzvah with his own hands, and so is it fitting for every person to do. And our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, said that one who exerts himself over matzat mitzvah until he sweats thereby brings about a kabbalistic rectification for the flaw of “keri” [seminal emission]. One who kneads after the prohibition of chametz [has taken effect] should say, at the start of the kneading, that all crumbs that fall during the kneading and rolling, and likewise the dough that sticks to the vessels, shall be ownerless like the dust of the earth. The custom is to set aside lulav branches to fuel the oven for the baking of matzat mitzvah. And this mitzvah is best performed by kneading and baking it on the eve of Pesach after seven-thirty – see “Birkei Yosef,” of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: The Rosh would exert himself to make matzat mitzvah with his own hands, and so is it fitting for every person to do. The Ari, of blessed memory, said that the exertion of sweating while making matzat mitzvah serves as a kabbalistic rectification for the flaw of “keri.” One who kneads after the prohibition of chametz has begun should declare at the start of the kneading that all crumbs that fall and dough that sticks to the vessels are ownerless like dust. The custom is to save lulav branches to fuel the oven, and it is best to knead and bake on the eve of Pesach after seven-thirty.
takeaways: It is fitting to make matzat mitzvah oneself, and to declare the crumbs ownerless
According to the Ari, of blessed memory, the sweat from the exertion of kneading serves as a kabbalistic rectification for the flaw of “keri”
It is best to knead and bake on the eve of Pesach after seven-thirty

paragraphs: If a whole grain of wheat is found in the matzah while it is still raw dough – if it is not split open, one removes from the matzah the amount that occupied its space, and the matzah itself is permitted; but if it is split open, the entire matzah in which the wheat grain was found becomes forbidden. However, if the wheat grain is found in the dough [before baking], even if split open, one removes only the amount that occupied its space and throws it into the fire, and the entire batch of dough is permitted, since this would otherwise involve a great loss, and it is also a time of pressing need – as I have written in my small book “Mikabtzi’el.”

clarification.explanation: If a wheat grain is found in the matzah while it is still raw and not split open, one removes the amount that occupied its space and the entire matzah is permitted; but if it is split open, the entire matzah in which it was found becomes forbidden. But if the grain is found in the dough [before baking], even if split open, one removes only the amount that occupied its space and throws it into the fire, and the entire batch of dough is permitted, because of the great loss involved and the pressing circumstance.
takeaways: A split wheat grain in a raw matzah forbids it; in the dough itself, only its own space is removed

paragraphs: It is forbidden to perform work on the eve of Pesach from midday onward, even without pay. One must get a haircut before midday, and if he forgot [and did not get one] before midday, he may get a haircut afterward through a non-Jew, but a Jew must stand over him to watch from the beginning of the haircut to the end. And even the cutting of fingernails – it is good to be careful to cut them before midday.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to perform work on the eve of Pesach from midday onward, even without payment. One must get a haircut before midday, and if he forgot, he may get one after midday through a non-Jew, provided a Jew stands over him and watches from the start of the haircut to its end. It is also good to cut one's fingernails before midday.
takeaways: No work on the eve of Pesach from midday onward; get a haircut and cut fingernails before midday

paragraphs: The firstborn, even if they are Kohanim or Levites, fast on the eve of Pesach – whether a firstborn from the father’s side or the mother’s side – but only males; the custom is that females do not fast. Even a male born after a stillbirth (nefel) must also fast. But one born after a child that died within thirty days of birth, whose months [of gestation] had been completed, need not fast, since one may rely in this on the Gaon “Shevut Yaakov” and the Gaon “Dagul MeRevavah,” who are lenient in this matter. And if the firstborn himself was the groom, or the father of a child [about to be circumcised], or a sandak [one who holds the baby at a brit], it is permitted for him to eat, and he need not make up his fast afterward; but if he happens to have a pidyon haben (redemption of his own son) to perform, he may not eat. Some have the custom that the groom invites the firstborns to dine with him that day at his wedding feast, and likewise the father of the child at the feast of the brit, and we do not protest against those who follow this custom; however, he may not invite many, but only enough to complete the [minyan of] ten, and no more – see “Chok Yaakov.” And at a siyum masechet (completion celebration of a tractate of Talmud), if the firstborn understands and grasps what is said at the time of the siyum, he is permitted to eat there – see “Chayim LeRosh.”

clarification.explanation: Firstborns, even Kohanim and Levites, fast on the eve of Pesach - whether firstborn to the father or to the mother - but only males, not females. Even a male born after a stillbirth (a fetus whose months were not completed) must fast. But a male born after a child that completed its months and died within thirty days of birth need not fast, relying on the lenient authorities (the responsa Shevut Yaakov and the Dagul MeRevavah). If the firstborn is a groom, the father of a child [being circumcised], or a sandak, he may eat and need not make up the fast, but if he has a pidyon haben to perform he may not eat. Some have the custom that the groom invites firstborns to his feast, and likewise the father of the child at a brit feast, but only a limited number, enough to complete a minyan of ten. And likewise at a siyum masechet, if the firstborn understands what is said, he may eat there.
takeaways: Male firstborns fast on the eve of Pesach, including one born after a stillbirth
A male born after a child that completed its months and died within thirty days is exempt from the fast, per the lenient authorities
A firstborn participating in a se'udat mitzvah (wedding, brit, siyum) is exempt from the fast

paragraphs: It is forbidden to say “this meat is for Pesach,” but rather one should say “this meat is for Yom Tov.” And it is forbidden to eat matzah on the eve of Pesach, and also on the night before the eve of Pesach one should not eat it; however, cooked matzah that was cooked before the fourteenth is permitted to be eaten on the fourteenth – so have I concluded in a responsum in my holy book “Rav Pe’alim.” And one should not eat much on the eve of Pesach, so that he will eat at the Seder night with appetite, like one who is expecting a guest, and so on.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to say “this meat is for Pesach,” rather “this meat is for Yom Tov.” It is forbidden to eat matzah on the eve of Pesach, and also on the night before it, but cooked matzah that was cooked before the fourteenth is permitted to be eaten on the fourteenth. And one should not eat much on the eve of Pesach, so as to eat on Seder night with appetite.
takeaways: One does not say “meat for Pesach” but “for Yom Tov”
Matzah is not eaten on the eve of Pesach; and one does not eat much, so as to eat at the Seder with appetite

paragraphs: Women must be careful in checking the lettuce (chazeret) and celery (karpas) [for insects], for [eating] any insect carries the liability of five sets of lashes. This matter rests upon the neck of the woman of the house, since all the members of the household rely upon her in this; and if she is lenient in her checking, it is possible that the liability of lashes hanging over her neck will be more numerous than the hairs of her head – especially when the members of the household are many, and in these places where tiny insects are commonly found in the vegetables. There is a story of a certain sage who entered a courtyard on the eve of Pesach and saw the woman of the house, before whom stood two large baskets full of lettuce, and she was washing the leaves of the lettuce and inspecting them quickly and superficially and placing them in a basket before her. The sage said to her: “How many hairs are on your head?” She said to him, “I have not counted them, and in my opinion it is impossible to count them.” He said to her, “The hairs of your head can indeed be counted, but the liability of lashes hanging over your neck cannot be counted.” She said to him, “What shall I do? The members of the household are many and want to eat much lettuce, for it is pleasing to them.” He said to her, “This answer will not save you on the Day of Judgment. Therefore, heed my advice: discard the leaves that require extensive checking, and take specifically the stalks [instead], and likewise check the celery only in a small amount, sufficient to fulfill one’s obligation exactly.” Therefore, a household with many diners where extensive checking is not done should act accordingly, and the custom is not to eat lettuce on the eve of Pesach; and likewise outside the Land [of Israel] one does not eat lettuce on the first day of Pesach.

clarification.explanation: Women must be very careful in checking lettuce and celery for insects, since any insect carries a liability of five lashes, and the members of the household rely on the woman of the house in this. A story is brought of a sage who rebuked a woman who checked leaves quickly, telling her that the liability of lashes hanging over her neck exceeds the hairs of her head, and he advised her to discard the leaves requiring extensive checking and take only the stalks. Therefore, in a household with many diners where thorough checking is not done, one should do the same. And the custom is not to eat lettuce on the eve of Pesach.
takeaways: Lettuce and celery are checked well for insects
In a large household - it is preferable to take stalks instead of leaves; lettuce is not eaten on the eve of Pesach

paragraphs: His table should be set from before nightfall, so that he can recite Kiddush immediately when it grows dark, that is, after the stars come out. He should drink all four cups while reclining, and all of them require dilution [with water], and he should perform the dilution with water in three separate pourings, one after another. The head of the household should have his cup poured for him by one of the household members, in a manner of freedom, and he should also receive the cup with both his hands from the two hands of the one giving it. Also, the eating of all four ke-zayit portions of matzah should be done while reclining, both by men and women, both by adults and children, and the reclining must be on the left side – and even a left-handed person reclines on the left like everyone else, and not, as one [authority] wrote, the reverse.

clarification.explanation: His table should be set from before nightfall so he can recite Kiddush immediately when it grows dark, after the stars come out. All four cups are drunk while reclining, and all require dilution with water in three separate pourings. The head of the household has his cup poured by a household member in a manner expressing freedom, and receives it with both hands from the giver's two hands. The eating of the four ke-zayit portions of matzah is likewise done while reclining - by men, women, adults, and children alike - and the reclining is on the left side, even for a left-handed person.
takeaways: The four cups and the matzah are eaten reclining on the left side
The cups are poured and received in a manner of freedom; even a left-handed person reclines on the left

paragraphs: One must drink most of the revi’it (quarter-measure) in one go, meaning in a single drinking, and should not break it up into two separate drinkings; but after the fact, even if he paused several times, he has fulfilled his obligation – only he should not let more time elapse from the start of the drinking to its end than the time it takes to drink a revi’it. The weight of a revi’it is twenty-seven dirhams. As a preferred practice one should drink the entire revi’it, but after the fact, if he drank most of a revi’it, he has fulfilled his obligation, as mentioned by the halachic authorities. And even though one does not recite the concluding blessing (borei nefashot) after drinking most of a revi’it, since there is a dispute about this and a doubt about blessings is resolved leniently – nonetheless, on the night of Pesach, where there are four cups and the concluding blessing pertains to all of them together, if in one or two of them he drank a full revi’it, he may afterward recite the concluding blessing; but if he did not drink a full revi’it in any one of them, he should not recite the concluding blessing over the wine, since a doubt about blessings is resolved leniently. Therefore, he should push himself to drink at least in one cup a full revi’it, and if the cup contains several revi’iyot he must drink the majority of it. And all four cups require rinsing and washing, so that he wash them inside and out each time.

clarification.explanation: One must drink most of the revi'it in one go, without a break, and after the fact he has fulfilled his obligation even if he paused, provided he did not take longer overall than the time it takes to drink a revi'it (the weight of a revi'it is twenty-seven dirhams). As a preferred practice one drinks the whole revi'it, and after the fact, most of it. Regarding the concluding blessing: on Pesach night, if he drank a full revi'it in one of the cups, he blesses afterward; if he did not drink a full revi'it in any cup, he does not bless. Therefore he should push himself to drink at least one full revi'it in one cup. All the cups require rinsing and washing each time.
takeaways: Most of the revi'it is drunk in one go, without a break
One should take care to drink at least a full revi'it in one cup, for the sake of the concluding blessing

paragraphs: They bring before the head of the household a plate containing three matzot, maror, charoset, karpas, a shank bone (zeroa), and an egg. The charoset is a remembrance of the mortar with which our forefathers were enslaved, and therefore nuts and almonds are placed within it. The zeroa is a remembrance of the Pesach [offering], since in the time of the Beit HaMikdash one would also bring the Pesach offering at the time of reciting the Haggadah, and the egg is a remembrance of the chagigah offering. Our custom is to make the zeroa roasted and the egg boiled in water. And if he forgot and did not roast the zeroa on the eve of Pesach, it is permitted to roast it on the night of Pesach, even though roasted meat is not eaten even on the first day [of Yom Tov], as I have written in my small book “Mikabtzi’el.” One must be careful with all the eggs boiled in a pot on Pesach, to wash them first in cold water in a separate vessel by themselves, because here those who sell eggs buy them from the Arabs, who keep them together with their flour, and flour sticks to their shells; therefore one should wash them well beforehand, since on Pesach chametz is forbidden even in the tiniest amount.

clarification.explanation: They bring before the head of the household a plate with three matzot, maror, charoset, karpas, a zeroa, and an egg. The charoset is a remembrance of the mortar of the enslavement, so nuts and almonds are placed in it; the zeroa is a remembrance of the Pesach offering, and the egg a remembrance of the chagigah offering. Our custom is to roast the zeroa and boil the egg. If he forgot to roast the zeroa before Pesach, it is permitted to roast it on Pesach night. One must be careful to wash all the eggs boiled during Pesach first, in cold water in a separate vessel, since flour sometimes sticks to their shells and chametz on Pesach is forbidden even in the tiniest amount.
takeaways: The Seder plate is arranged with three matzot, maror, charoset, karpas, zeroa, and an egg
The eggs are washed of flour before cooking

paragraphs: One washes his hands for the sake of the first dipping, and should not recite a blessing over this washing. Praiseworthy is the one who is careful to wash his hands [before eating] a food dipped in liquid throughout the entire year, as the crown of our heads, my father, of blessed memory, was careful throughout the year and would warn many people about this – for in truth, the leniency common among the people in this matter during the rest of the year is based on a solitary opinion – see the responsa “Mateh Yosef,” of blessed memory, what he wrote about this.

clarification.explanation: One washes his hands for the first dipping and does not recite a blessing over this washing. Praiseworthy is one who is careful to wash his hands before eating any food dipped in liquid throughout the entire year, as the author's father was careful and would warn others about this, since the common leniency in this matter during the rest of the year is based on a solitary opinion.
takeaways: Hands are washed for the first dipping, without a blessing
It is fitting to be careful about washing hands for [food] dipped in liquid all year round

paragraphs: He should take karpas less than a ke-zayit [in volume], so that he not become obligated in a concluding blessing, and recite over it “Borei peri ha’adamah,” intending thereby to exempt the maror as well; he dips it in vinegar and eats it without reclining, as the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, wrote, and so has been our custom since the time of the crown of our heads, my grandfather, of blessed memory, to eat it without reclining. This first dipping, which is karpas in vinegar, is a remembrance of the cause of the harsh servitude that came about through the sale of Joseph the Righteous, peace be upon him, and their dipping his coat of many colors in blood and selling him, causing anguish to our father Jacob, peace be upon him; and this is hinted at in the word “karpas” – the letters “kar” are the end [letters] of “mechar” (sale), and the letters “pas” are the beginning [letters] of “passim” (the coat of many colors). And the second dipping, maror in charoset, is a remembrance of the harsh servitude itself, since they embittered their lives through the labor of the mortar hinted at in the charoset – as I have written on this in my small book “Mikabtzi’el.” And even though we said that one must take karpas less than a ke-zayit so as not to become obligated in a concluding blessing, if he erred and ate a ke-zayit, he must recite “Borei nefashot rabbot” afterward; nevertheless, he should not recite “Borei peri ha’adamah” over the maror [later], since it is considered part of the requirements of the meal that come within the meal [and thus exempted by the earlier blessing]. And he should be careful not to eat all the karpas that is on the plate, but rather some karpas should remain on the plate until after HaMotzi, since the “secret of the plate” must remain intact until after the eating of matzah and maror.

clarification.explanation: One takes karpas less than a ke-zayit so as not to become obligated in a concluding blessing, blesses “Borei peri ha'adamah” and intends to exempt the maror as well, dips it in vinegar, and eats it without reclining. The first dipping - karpas in vinegar - is a remembrance of the harsh servitude that came about through the sale of Joseph (“kar” being the end of “mechar” - sale, and “pas” the beginning of “passim” - the coat of many colors), and the second dipping (maror in charoset) is a remembrance of the servitude itself. If he mistakenly ate a ke-zayit of karpas, he must recite “Borei nefashot” afterward; nevertheless he should not recite “Borei peri ha'adamah” over the maror, since it is considered among the requirements of the meal that come within it. He should be careful to leave some karpas on the plate until after HaMotzi, since the “secret of the plate” must remain intact until after the eating of matzah and maror.
takeaways: Karpas less than a ke-zayit, “Borei peri ha'adamah” with intent to exempt the maror, without reclining
Some karpas is left on the plate until after HaMotzi, and the “secret of the plate” remains intact until after the eating of matzah and maror

paragraphs: He takes the middle matzah and divides it into two: he gives the larger half to one of those present to put away for the afikoman, and places the smaller half between the two whole matzot. And according to the [kabbalistic] secret, he should divide the middle matzah so as to form the shape of the letters “dalet” and “vav”: the piece shaped like a “vav” he sets aside for the afikoman, and the piece shaped like a “dalet” he places between the matzot. When he recites “Ha lachma anya,” he lifts up the broken piece, and says “Ha” with a tzeirei vowel, and our custom is to repeat this passage three times. Afterward he instructs that the plate be placed at the end of the table, and the cup should be poured and placed before him so that [the children] will ask, “Mah Nishtanah.” When he begins to say “Avadim hayinu,” the plate is brought before him again. And when he says “Ein maftirin achar hapesach afikoman” (“One does not conclude the meal after the Pesach offering with an afikoman”), it is a fine custom to hold up the half-matzah hidden away for the afikoman, to show those present that it is a remembrance of the Pesach [offering], as mentioned in the book “Tanya.” And when he reaches “Matzah zo” (“This matzah”), he lifts up the whole upper matzah before him, out of endearment for the mitzvah, and likewise the law when he reaches “Maror zeh” (“This maror”). But when he says “Pesach she’hayu avoteinu ochlim” (“the Pesach offering that our forefathers used to eat”), he does not hold the zeroa in his hand, but only shows it. And when he reaches “Hi she’amdah,” he holds the cup that was poured for him in his hand, and he covers the bread; and one should be careful to cover the bread every time he takes the cup in his hand.

clarification.explanation: He takes the middle matzah and divides it in two: the larger half is given to be put away for the afikoman, and the smaller placed between the two whole matzot. And according to the kabbalistic secret, he divides the middle matzah so as to form the shape of two letters - dalet and vav: the piece shaped like the vav is set aside for the afikoman, and the piece shaped like the dalet remains between the matzot. When he says “Ha lachma anya” he lifts the broken piece, and says “Ha” with a tzeirei (and our custom is to repeat this passage three times). Afterward he instructs that the plate be placed at the end of the table, and the cup poured and placed before him so that the children will ask “Mah Nishtanah”; and when he begins “Avadim hayinu,” the plate is brought before him again. And when he says “Ein maftirin achar hapesach afikoman,” it is a fine custom to hold up the half-matzah hidden for the afikoman and show it to those present as a remembrance of the Pesach offering. When he reaches “Matzah zo” and “Maror zeh,” he lifts them up, but the zeroa (in the passage about the Pesach offering) he only shows, without holding it up. And when he reaches “Hi she'amdah” he holds the cup, and covers the bread - and one should remember to cover the bread whenever the cup is held.
takeaways: The dividing of the middle matzah is done according to the kabbalistic secret, forming the shape of the letters dalet-vav: the vav-piece for the afikoman, and the dalet-piece remaining between the matzot
The broken piece is lifted up while reciting “Ha lachma anya,” and the custom is to repeat this passage three times
At “Matzah zo” and “Maror zeh,” these are lifted up; the zeroa (in the passage about the Pesach offering) is only shown, without lifting
Whenever the cup is held (as at “Hi she'amdah”), one must remember to cover the bread

paragraphs: He washes his hands and recites the blessing over the washing of hands, takes all three matzot together for the sake of “lechem mishneh” (double bread), recites “HaMotzi,” sets aside the third one, and is left holding the top matzah and the broken one. He recites the blessing “concerning the eating of matzah,” and breaks off a ke-zayit from this one and a ke-zayit from that one – each ke-zayit being nine dirhams – dips them in salt three times, and eats them while reclining. He puts these two ke-zayit portions into his mouth together, so that he eats from both of them at once; and if he is prevented and cannot do so, and wishes instead to crumble each ke-zayit into small pieces to put into his mouth, he should then put in the crumbs of the whole ke-zayit [matzah] first, as mentioned by the Acharonim. Afterward he takes a ke-zayit of maror and dips it into the charoset, and shakes off a little of the charoset, since the taste of the maror is required; he recites the blessing “concerning the eating of maror,” and this does not require reclining. Then he immediately takes the third matzah, breaks off a ke-zayit from it, wraps it together with a ke-zayit of maror, and dips it in charoset, saying “A remembrance of the Beit HaMikdash, in the manner of Hillel the Elder,” and eats them while reclining. He should be careful not to speak of unrelated matters between the eating of the matzah and the eating of the “korech” (the wrap); therefore he should eat them one right after the other, immediately, without delay. Afterward he continues and completes his meal with joy and a glad heart.

clarification.explanation: He washes his hands with a blessing, takes the three matzot together for the sake of “lechem mishneh,” recites “HaMotzi,” sets aside the third, and recites “concerning the eating of matzah” over the top matzah and the broken one. He breaks off a ke-zayit from each (a ke-zayit being nine dirhams), dips them in salt three times, and eats them together while reclining. Afterward he eats a ke-zayit of maror dipped in charoset (shaking off a little of the charoset so the taste of maror remains), recites “concerning the eating of maror,” without reclining. Then he immediately takes a ke-zayit from the third matzah, wraps it with maror and charoset, says “A remembrance of the Beit HaMikdash, in the manner of Hillel,” and eats it while reclining, without speaking between the eating of the matzah and the korech.
takeaways: HaMotzi and matzah are eaten as two ke-zayit portions while reclining; maror dipped in charoset is eaten without reclining
The korech is eaten while reclining, immediately, without speaking between the matzah and the korech

paragraphs: After he finishes his meal, he joyfully eats the afikoman that was kept, as a remembrance of the Pesach offering that was eaten while satiated; therefore he should be careful not to eat much during the meal, so that he eat the afikoman with appetite. He should eat two ke-zayit portions of it, as the preferred way of performing the mitzvah: one ke-zayit as a remembrance of the Pesach offering, and one ke-zayit as a remembrance of the matzah eaten together with the Pesach offering. And if he is elderly or very weak and it is difficult for him to eat two ke-zayit portions, he should eat one ke-zayit specifically as a remembrance of the Pesach offering. He must eat it in one place, and not in two places – and even in one room but at two [separate] tables it is forbidden. He should be careful to eat it before midnight, and it is good that the Hallel also be recited before midnight. He should not doze off in the middle of eating the afikoman; and if he is reclining alone at the table, even during the meal before eating the afikoman, he should not sleep – see “Shulchan Gavoah,” of blessed memory. After the afikoman one should not eat anything else, since the taste of the afikoman must remain in his mouth until he goes to sleep; only water is permitted to drink, and some permit coffee, and one may rely on them in a case of great need. As for the drinking of smoke [tobacco] – there, Rabbi Chaim Palagi, in “Chayim LeRosh,” agreed to caution against it on the first night, but permitted it on the second night. And what is called “afikoman” is a Greek-derived acronym for “afiku minei” [meaning] that they should not eat anything more; and the crown of our heads, my father, of blessed memory, explained “afiku man” as an acronym for “mayin nukvin” (feminine waters) that rise up from the mitzvah of eating this matzah, this eating being the final mitzvah, and these are the words of the wise, [spoken] gracefully.

clarification.explanation: After the meal, he joyfully eats the afikoman that was kept, as a remembrance of the Pesach offering eaten while satiated; therefore he should not eat much during the meal, so as to eat the afikoman with appetite. He eats two ke-zayit portions (one for the Pesach offering, one for the matzah eaten with it), and an elderly or very weak person eats one ke-zayit, specifically for the Pesach offering. He eats it in one place, before midnight, and does not doze off in the middle. After the afikoman nothing is eaten, so that its taste remains in his mouth until he falls asleep; only water may be drunk (and some permit coffee for great need), and smoking - forbidden on the first night, permitted on the second. The name “afikoman” is explained as a Greek-derived acronym for “afiku minei” (do not eat anything else), and the author's father explained it as “afiku man” - an acronym for “mayin nukvin” arising from the mitzvah of eating this matzah, the final mitzvah.
takeaways: The afikoman (two ke-zayit portions) is eaten in one place, before midnight, with appetite
Nothing is eaten afterward; only water is permitted (some permit coffee); smoking is forbidden on the first night and permitted on the second
The name “afikoman” is expounded as a Greek-derived acronym: “afiku minei” (do not eat any more), and also “afiku man” - an acronym for “mayin nukvin”

paragraphs: If one forgot to eat the afikoman and only remembered after washing his hands [for Grace after Meals], or after saying “Hav lan u’nevareich,” he should eat it without the blessing of HaMotzi. And if he did not remember until after reciting the Grace after Meals, and he had not yet drunk the third cup, he should wash his hands, recite HaMotzi, and eat the afikoman. And if he had already drunk the third cup and only then remembered – if he had eaten during the meal a ke-zayit’s measure from that matzah which was guarded from the time of the harvest [shmurah matzah], he may rely on that; but if not, then if he did not remember until after the Hallel, he should wash his hands, recite HaMotzi, eat the afikoman, and then go back and recite the blessing over the cup – see “Beit David,” siman 259, page 70, and “Shulchan Gavoah,” siman 476, se’if katan 8, to be examined there.

clarification.explanation: If one forgot to eat the afikoman and remembered after washing his hands or saying “Hav lan u'nevareich,” he eats it without the blessing of HaMotzi. If he remembered after Grace after Meals but before the third cup, he washes his hands, recites HaMotzi, and eats it. If he had already drunk the third cup, and he ate a ke-zayit of shmurah matzah during the meal, he may rely on that; if not, and he only remembered after the Hallel, he washes his hands, recites HaMotzi, eats the afikoman, and then returns to recite the blessing over the cup.
takeaways: Forgetting the afikoman - the order of correction depends on whether he has already recited Grace after Meals or drunk the third cup

paragraphs: A person is obligated to recount the miracles and wonders that the Lord, blessed be He, performed for us and for our forefathers, until sleep overtakes him. And it is stated in the holy Zohar (Ra’aya Mehemna, Parashat Bo): It is a commandment to recount the Exodus from Egypt, and the Holy One, blessed be He, rejoices in this recounting, as does the entire heavenly retinue, and He says to them, “Go and hear this praise from below” – and through this recounting the heavens are split open and strength is given to their Master. From this we derive the general principle that one who recounts much of the Exodus from Egypt is praiseworthy in the heavenly retinue, that the Holy One, blessed be He, glories in him, as it is written (Isaiah 49:3), “Israel, in whom I take glory.”

clarification.explanation: A person is obligated to recount the miracles and wonders that God performed for us and our forefathers, until sleep overtakes him. The holy Zohar teaches that the Holy One rejoices in this recounting and gathers the heavenly retinue to hear the praise of Israel from below, and through this recounting the heavens are split open and strength is granted above. Therefore, one who recounts much of the Exodus is praiseworthy, for the Holy One glories in him.
takeaways: One recounts the Exodus until overcome by sleep
One who recounts much is praiseworthy - the Holy One glories in Israel

paragraphs: One must recite the Shema on retiring, with the verses customarily recited every night, in the order of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory. And if he stays awake until after midnight, he should recite it a little before midnight. And outside the Land [of Israel], all the laws of the first night apply likewise to the second night; and one must recite Shehecheyanu outside the Land on both of the first two nights of Pesach at Kiddush, but on the last nights, which are the seventh and eighth days of Pesach, one does not recite Shehecheyanu at Kiddush. And when reciting Shehecheyanu on the first night, one should also intend it for the eating of matzah.

clarification.explanation: One recites the Shema on retiring with the verses customary every night, in the order of the Ari, of blessed memory; if he stays awake past midnight he should recite it a little before midnight. Outside the Land, all the laws of the first night apply also to the second night, and Shehecheyanu is recited at Kiddush on both of the first two nights, but not on the last nights (the seventh and eighth days). When reciting Shehecheyanu on the first night, one should also intend it for the eating of matzah.
takeaways: The Shema on retiring follows the order of the Ari
Outside the Land, Shehecheyanu is recited only on the first two nights; one intends it also for the matzah

paragraphs: One passing by a non-Jewish baker on Pesach should not smell the hot bread. And I found it written that one does not strike dogs during the festival of Pesach, and especially on the first and second days, on which the Exodus from Egypt is recounted – and even though our Sages, of blessed memory, said of the dog (Shabbat 155b), “Anoint its ear and take a stick after it,” one should remove the stick from over them during Pesach, since on the night of Pesach, at the Exodus from Egypt, it is written, “no dog shall whet its tongue” – that they observed His, blessed be He’s, decree on that night; therefore the Torah says [regarding an unfit carcass], “You shall throw it to the dog.”

clarification.explanation: One passing by a non-Jew's bakery on Pesach should not smell the hot bread. And it is found written that dogs are not struck during the festival of Pesach, especially on the first and second days, since on the night of the Exodus it is written “no dog shall whet its tongue” - the dogs observed God's decree on that night; therefore the Torah says regarding an unfit carcass, “You shall throw it to the dog.”
takeaways: One does not smell hot bread from a non-Jew on Pesach
The custom is not to strike dogs on Pesach, as a reward for their restraint on the night of the Exodus

paragraphs: Raisin sellers should watch their sacks so that there is no actual chametz in the sacks – since chametz tends to stick to them, because in the place where the raisins [are stored], flour is commonly used there, and water gets on the sacks and the sack becomes soiled with the flour, which becomes actual chametz. And one who raises chickens should clear their coop of barley, and should buy for them before Pesach millet or dhurra (sorghum), and begin feeding them this before Pesach enters. It is permitted to buy chickens during Pesach, provided he states explicitly that he does not wish to buy the crop [gizzard] at all; and after slaughtering, he should open it immediately and throw the crop outside – see “Shiyurei Berachah” and “Tuv Ayin.” And here in our city there are several householders who do not eat chickens at all during Pesach, as a protective fence, out of concern that wheat and barley might be found in them; and one who wishes to eat chicken due to some pressing reason should have his personal custom [of abstention] annulled – see “Lev Chaim,” part 2, siman 207.

clarification.explanation: Raisin sellers should watch that their sacks contain no actual chametz, since flour is used where the raisins are kept and can become chametz when moistened. One who raises chickens should clear their coop of barley and feed them millet or sorghum before Pesach. It is permitted to buy chickens during Pesach, provided one states he does not wish to buy the crop [gizzard] at all, and throws it out immediately after slaughtering. Some householders in this city do not eat chicken at all during Pesach as a protective measure, out of concern for wheat or barley in the crop, and one who wishes to eat it for a pressing reason should have his personal custom annulled.
takeaways: The chicken coop is cleared of barley and the birds are fed sorghum before Pesach
One who buys a chicken during Pesach stipulates not buying the crop, and discards it immediately

paragraphs: Here in our city there are many householders who have the custom not to eat rice on Pesach, because rice may contain a mixture of wheat and barley grains, and it must first be checked two or three times, and there is concern that they may err in checking, and wheat or barley may remain in the rice and be cooked in it – therefore they abstain from it. And some have the custom of eating it after checking. Therefore, if the head of the household eats rice, but his cook has the custom of not eating rice, it is forbidden for the cook to cook rice on Yom Tov for the head of the household, since he [the cook] observes a prohibition in his own eating as a protective fence; however, it is permitted to carry it [move it] on Yom Tov. So have I concluded, with God’s help, in a responsum in my holy book “Rav Pe’alim.” And the same applies in other cases on Yom Tov: if this cook ate meat on Yom Tov, it is forbidden for him to cook dairy for others unless there remains enough time in the day for six hours to pass after eating the meat, so that it would be fitting for him to eat from that dish that same day; but if there is not enough time in the day for him to eat from it himself, it is forbidden for him to cook it for others – however, carrying it is permitted.

clarification.explanation: In Baghdad many have the custom not to eat rice on Pesach out of concern for a mixture of wheat and barley that is difficult to check for, and some have the custom of eating it after checking. Therefore, if the head of the household eats rice but the cook observes a prohibition against it, it is forbidden for the cook to cook rice on Yom Tov for the head of the household (though carrying it is permitted). The same applies on other Yom Tovim: a cook who ate meat may not cook dairy for others unless there remains enough time in the day for him to eat from that dish himself after six hours have passed - but carrying it is permitted.
takeaways: The custom in Baghdad is to abstain from rice on Pesach out of concern for a mixture
One who personally observes a prohibition does not cook that same food for another, though carrying it is permitted
