paragraphs: One should not drink milk from a non-Jew’s animal on Pesach, lest he fed it chametz. And if one takes leaven (se’or) from a non-Jew after Pesach, one should be careful to separate from that dough a challah portion that is larger than the measure of the entire leaven.

clarification.explanation: One does not drink milk from a non-Jew's animal on Pesach, lest he fed it chametz. And if leaven is taken from a non-Jew after Pesach, one should be careful to separate from that dough a challah larger than the measure of the entire leaven.
takeaways: Milk from a non-Jew's animal is not drunk on Pesach
Leaven from a non-Jew after Pesach - a challah portion larger than the whole leaven is separated

paragraphs: One does not recite Tikkun Leah during the intermediate days (Chol HaMoed) of Pesach, and one should be careful throughout all the days of the festival to occupy oneself with Torah, which gives life to those who practice it, in this world and the World to Come.

clarification.explanation: Tikkun Leah (Tikkun Chatzot) is not recited during Chol HaMoed of Pesach. One should be careful throughout all the days of the festival to occupy oneself with Torah, which gives life to those who practice it, in this world and the next.
takeaways: Tikkun Leah is not recited during Chol HaMoed of Pesach
One occupies oneself with Torah throughout all the days of the festival

paragraphs: [This applies when the eve of Pesach falls on Shabbat.] One checks for chametz on the night of the thirteenth, following the same laws we wrote above for the search on the night of the fourteenth. And the firstborns fast on Thursday. Therefore, if the one performing the search is a firstborn, he should taste some fruit or a food made from the five grains before the blessing, so that he search with a settled and calm mind. After the search he nullifies the chametz as we wrote regarding the night of the fourteenth; but the nullification for the day, he should not perform on Friday, but rather on Shabbat itself – and he should be careful not to forget this. However, the burning of the chametz he should do on Friday, burning the pieces he does not wish to eat, and setting aside bread for the Shabbat evening meal and the Shabbat morning meal. And the burning on the eve of Pesach should be done before midday, in the same manner as is done on the fourteenth when it falls on a weekday, so that people not come to err in other years.

clarification.explanation: When Erev Pesach falls on Shabbat, one checks for chametz on the night of the thirteenth, following the same laws as the search on the night of the fourteenth. The firstborns fast on Thursday. If the searcher is a firstborn, he should taste fruit or grain-based food before the blessing, so as to search calmly. After the search he nullifies the chametz, but he does not perform the daytime nullification on Friday - rather on Shabbat itself (and he should be careful not to forget). The burning is done on Friday before midday, setting aside bread for the Shabbat meals.
takeaways: When Erev Pesach falls on Shabbat: the search is on the night of the thirteenth; firstborns fast on Thursday
The burning is done on Friday before midday; the daytime nullification is postponed to Shabbat

paragraphs: On the Shabbat that precedes, which is the fourteenth day, they should hasten to pray in the morning, so as to go out quickly to eat the morning meal, so that they not stumble into the prohibition of eating chametz on the eve of Pesach after its permitted time; however, they should be careful not to pray in haste and rushed. And if there are grooms [being called up] on that Shabbat, the fathers of the sons [being celebrated] should not invite many guests for the Torah aliyot as is their usual custom, so as not to prolong the time [of the service] thereby – since they must go out quickly to eat the morning meal. They should hasten to recite Kiddush and eat immediately, and should eat all the chametz they have in the house before the prohibition of eating it takes effect; and if any chametz remains that they cannot eat, they should give it to a non-Jew, and not throw it into the public domain. And on this Shabbat one should not cook a dish that tends to stick greatly to the pot such that it cannot be wiped off with a finger, so as not to need to rinse the pots and plates; however, if he did cook such a dish and it stuck to the pot, it is permitted to rinse the pot with water by hand, but not with a rag, because of the prohibition of wringing on Shabbat – and this rinsing is considered somewhat a need of the day, since there is a mitzvah-related need involved, as the “Pri Chadash,” “Knesset HaGedolah,” and “Shulchan Gavoah” wrote; but if it is possible to wipe it off with a finger, it is forbidden to rinse it, as mentioned in “Eliyah Rabbah” and other Acharonim. And after he finishes all his eating and no chametz remains with him, he then nullifies it, saying, “Kol chamira… d’chazitei ud’la chazitei.”

clarification.explanation: On the Shabbat that is the 14th, one hastens to pray in the morning in order to go out quickly to the morning meal, so as not to stumble into eating chametz after its permitted time (but without praying in haste). If there are grooms [being called up], the fathers should not invite many guests for the aliyot, so as not to prolong the service. They hasten to recite Kiddush and eat, finishing all their chametz before its prohibition takes effect; what remains is given to a non-Jew, not thrown into the public domain. On this Shabbat one should not cook a dish that sticks greatly to the pot; if it does stick, it is permitted to rinse the pot with water by hand (not with a rag, due to the prohibition of wringing). After finishing all his eating, with no chametz remaining, he nullifies it.
takeaways: One hastens to pray and eat before the time the chametz prohibition takes effect
One does not cook a dish that sticks to the pot; the chametz is nullified after the meal

paragraphs: He should eat the night meal and the morning meal on this Shabbat specifically in one place in the courtyard, and should not make many crumbs on the table at night or in the morning; and if crumbs are made, he should watch over them to eat them immediately, before a liquid falls on them and they become repulsive. After eating them, they should shake out the table or the tablecloth into the public domain, on account of tiny crumbs that cannot be gathered by hand to be eaten; also, after eating, they should sweep the place where they ate, on account of any crumbs that fell, and should throw the sweepings into the public domain and not leave the sweepings in the trash heap in his courtyard. It is permitted to eat eggs on this Shabbat at the morning meal, and there is no concern in this regarding the eating of eggs on the night of Pesach, since this is not comparable to lettuce and the like; however, some have the custom not to eat eggs on this Shabbat at the morning meal, because they place an egg in the plate on the night of Pesach and eat it as a remembrance of the chagigah offering – and everyone should follow his own custom in this matter.

clarification.explanation: The night meal and morning meal on this Shabbat are eaten in one place only, and one should avoid making many crumbs; if crumbs are made, they are watched and eaten immediately. After eating, the table or cloth is shaken out into the public domain, and the eating place is swept, with the sweepings thrown into the public domain rather than left in the courtyard's trash heap. It is permitted to eat eggs at the morning meal on this Shabbat, though some abstain because an egg is placed on the Seder plate as a remembrance of the chagigah offering - and everyone follows his own custom.
takeaways: Eating in one place, and being careful to clean up all crumbs of chametz
It is permitted to eat eggs at the morning meal; some abstain, following their custom

paragraphs: Festival garments should be put on this Shabbat after Minchah, and one should also change one’s shirt after Minchah, because chametz was eaten while wearing it at night and in the morning, and there is concern that some small crumb of chametz may have stuck to it; but there is no such concern regarding trousers and a tallit. And one who is poor and has only one shirt, which he wore on Shabbat night, should be careful while eating to tuck the sleeve inward, and after eating he should check his shirt.

clarification.explanation: Festival garments are put on this Shabbat after Minchah, and one also changes his shirt after Minchah, since chametz was eaten while wearing it and a small crumb might have stuck to it; but there is no such concern regarding trousers and a tallit. A poor person who has only one shirt should tuck the sleeve inward while eating, and check the shirt afterward.
takeaways: One changes the shirt and puts on festival garments after Minchah
A poor person with only one shirt tucks in the sleeve and checks it after eating

paragraphs: The third meal (Seudah Shlishit) should be made with fruit after Minchah, and it is good to make it with fruits whose concluding blessing is “Me’ein Shalosh” (of the three-fold type). They are brought before him on a plate on the table, and he also says, before eating, “Atkinu se’udata” and so on, as on any other Shabbat. He should not eat much, so that he eat at night with appetite. On this Shabbat it is my custom to expound, with God’s help, in the synagogue on the Haggadah – but one must begin early, so that we pray at nine-thirty; and the sermon of Shabbat HaGadol [proper] is on the preceding Shabbat.

clarification.explanation: The third meal is made with fruit after Minchah, preferably fruit whose concluding blessing is “Me'ein Shalosh.” It is brought on a plate, with “Atkinu se'udata” recited as on any Shabbat, without eating much, so as to eat at night with appetite. On this Shabbat the author's custom is to expound in the synagogue on the Haggadah (beginning the prayers early, at nine-thirty), while the sermon proper for Shabbat HaGadol is given on the preceding Shabbat.
takeaways: The third meal is fruit (preferably “Me'ein Shalosh”) after Minchah, without eating much

paragraphs: The matzat mitzvah with which he will fulfill his obligation on the first night should not be moved on this Shabbat that falls on the eve of Pesach, since it is muktzeh, not fit for eating [on Shabbat itself], as he certainly is careful not to feed it even to children; but the other matzot, which are for the purpose of eating during the days of Pesach, are permitted to be moved on this Shabbat – for even though adults are forbidden to eat matzah on the eve of Pesach, nevertheless they are fit to be eaten by children.

clarification.explanation: The matzat mitzvah for the first night's obligation should not be moved on this Shabbat, since it is muktzeh, being unfit to eat (as one is certainly careful not to feed it even to children). But the other matzot, meant for eating during Pesach, are permitted to be moved on this Shabbat, since even though adults may not eat matzah on the eve of Pesach, it is fit for children to eat.
takeaways: The matzat mitzvah is muktzeh and forbidden to be moved on this Shabbat
The other matzot are permitted to be moved, since they are fit for children

paragraphs: The setting of the table for the sake of the night should not be done except after dark, since Shabbat does not prepare for Yom Tov; but once twilight has passed, that is, seven minutes after the call to the “Maghreb” [prayer], it is permitted to prepare for the sake of the night. And every person must sleep on this Shabbat after the morning meal, so that he can remain properly awake at night – and the same applies to women and children, who should be careful about this. And after he wakes from his sleep during the day, he should occupy himself with Torah, which gives life to those who practice it, and it is good to study Mishnah Pesachim.

clarification.explanation: The setting of the table for the night is not done until after dark, since Shabbat does not prepare for Yom Tov; but once twilight has passed (seven minutes after the call to Maghreb), it is permitted to prepare for the night. Every person - and likewise women and children - must sleep on this Shabbat after the morning meal, in order to stay properly awake at night. After waking, one should occupy himself with Torah, and it is good to study Mishnah Pesachim.
takeaways: Preparations for the Seder night are not made until after dark
One sleeps after the morning meal in order to stay awake for the Seder

paragraphs: One must make an eiruv tavshilin with bread and a cooked dish; the measure of the bread is 18 dirhams, and the measure of the cooked dish is 9 dirhams, and less than this does not suffice. It is good to make the cooked dish from hard-boiled eggs, since these keep in these places, which are hot; but meat will not keep for two nights and two days in the heat – for if Yom Tov falls on Thursday and Friday, the piece of meat would need to last for two days and two nights, that is, until Shabbat night; therefore it is good to use hard-boiled eggs, since these keep and do not spoil.

clarification.explanation: When Yom Tov falls adjacent to Shabbat, one must make an eiruv tavshilin with bread and a cooked dish: the bread measure is 18 dirhams and the cooked dish 9 dirhams, and less than this does not suffice. It is good to make the cooked dish from hard-boiled eggs, which keep in the heat, since meat will not last two days and two nights in the heat (when Yom Tov falls on Thursday and Friday and the dish must last until Shabbat night).
takeaways: Eiruv tavshilin: 18 dirhams of bread and 9 dirhams of cooked food
It is good to use hard-boiled eggs, which keep in the heat

paragraphs: He takes the eiruv in his hand and recites the blessing “…Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the mitzvah of eiruv,” [and says] “By virtue of this eiruv, may it be permitted for us to bake, cook, insulate, prepare, and light a lamp, and to do all that we need, from Yom Tov for Shabbat.” One who is a shochet [ritual slaughterer] should add the word “and to slaughter”; and if he did not add it, there is no harm, since this is included within “all that we need,” as our teacher Rabbeinu Zalman, of blessed memory, wrote. And it is a mitzvah to eat the eiruv at the Shabbat meal.

clarification.explanation: He takes the eiruv in his hand and recites the blessing “concerning the mitzvah of eiruv,” and says “By virtue of this eiruv, may it be permitted for us to bake, cook... and to do all that we need, from Yom Tov for Shabbat.” A shochet should add the word “and to slaughter,” though if he did not, it is included within “all that we need.” It is a mitzvah to eat the eiruv at the Shabbat meal.
takeaways: One recites the blessing and the formula for eiruv tavshilin
It is a mitzvah to eat the eiruv at the Shabbat meal

paragraphs: One must guard his eiruv so that it not be lost, and that it not be eaten before Shabbat night after dark. And if this should happen to him, or if he forgot and erred and did not set aside an eiruv – here in our city, may it be protected, he may rely on my eiruv, since I, the lowly one, acquire [merit] on behalf of and make an eiruv for all who err or are prevented, and for those whose eiruv becomes lost before Shabbat.

clarification.explanation: One must guard his eiruv so that it is not lost and not eaten before Shabbat night, after dark. If this happens, or if one forgot and did not make an eiruv at all, in Baghdad one may rely on the rabbi's eiruv, which he makes on behalf of all who err, are prevented, or whose eiruv is lost before Shabbat.
takeaways: The eiruv is guarded until Shabbat night
One who forgot or lost his eiruv may rely on the rabbi's general eiruv

paragraphs: If on the eve of Yom Tov one forgot to make an eiruv, and he [already] prayed the evening service, or said “Barechu” and then remembered – even though it is still day, he should not make an eiruv, but should rely on mine.

clarification.explanation: If one forgot to make an eiruv on the eve of Yom Tov, and had already prayed the evening service or said “Barechu” when he remembered - even though it is still technically day - he should not make an eiruv, but should rely on the rabbi's eiruv.
takeaways: One who has [effectively] accepted Yom Tov (evening prayer/Barechu) does not make an eiruv, but relies on the rabbi's eiruv

paragraphs: If Yom Tov falls on Thursday and Friday, even though one made an eiruv and cooks on Friday for the sake of Shabbat, nonetheless it is forbidden to cook on Thursday, which is the first day, for the sake of Shabbat.

clarification.explanation: If Yom Tov falls on Thursday and Friday, even though one made an eiruv and cooks on Friday for Shabbat, it is nonetheless forbidden to cook on Thursday, the first day, for the sake of Shabbat. The eiruv permits cooking only from the Yom Tov day adjacent to Shabbat.
takeaways: The eiruv permits cooking for Shabbat only from the Yom Tov day adjacent to it (Friday), not from Thursday

paragraphs: If there are three or four householders living in one courtyard, and among them are women or men who do not know how to make an eiruv, and only one among them knows how to make an eiruv, they should all bring their eiruv [bread and dish] to that one person among the residents who knows how to make an eiruv, and he should hold everything in his hand and say, “May it be permitted for us and for all who live in this courtyard.”

clarification.explanation: If three or four householders live in one courtyard, and among them are women or men who do not know how to make an eiruv, and only one knows how - they should all bring their eiruv to that one person, who holds it all in his hand and says, “May it be permitted for us and for all who live in this courtyard.”
takeaways: The one who knows how to make the eiruv acquires it on behalf of all the residents of the courtyard, holding all the eiruvin together

paragraphs: Regarding a head of household who is unlearned and does not know how to recite the text of the eiruv, and likewise a widow with young children who does not know how to recite the text of the eiruv – the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, wrote in “Chayim Sha’al,” part 1, page 94, that the custom in our holy city of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and established, is to send a pair of rabbis from the Beit Din to go around and make the eiruv tavshilin on behalf of widows and anyone else who does not know how, taking from them in each house bread and a cooked dish, and saying thus: “By virtue of this eiruv, may it be permitted for this head of household and all members of his household to bake, cook,” and so on – and this is done by way of agency (shelichut); see there. And regarding the blessing – if this unlearned person or the woman knows how to recite the blessing, and only does not know the text of the eiruv, I have concluded in a responsum in my holy book “Rav Pe’alim,” regarding the law of Chanukah, that the sick person may recite the blessing while lying in bed, and another may light [the candles] in front of him in his room – and there I brought the words of Rabbi “Chikrei Lev,” letter yud, part 2, siman 8, page 31, and the “Machatzit HaShekel” in the laws of Shabbat, siman 11, and the “Pri Chadash,” siman 432, and the words of the Rabbi on “Erech HaShulchan,” what he wrote in his book “Chukat HaPesach,” siman 432, regarding the words of the Rashal, of blessed memory – and although I brought there the words of Rabbi “Beit David,” of blessed memory, in the laws of Rosh Hashanah, siman 393, who wrote that one should not have one person perform [the act] and another recite the blessing, nevertheless I concluded, regarding the aforementioned law of Chanukah, that the head of the household who is sick recites the blessing and his agent lights – and the same applies here: this unlearned person may recite the blessing, and his agent standing beside him immediately recites the text of the eiruv.

clarification.explanation: A head of household who is unlearned and does not know the text of the eiruv, and likewise a widow who does not know it, [may be helped as follows]: the custom in Jerusalem is to send a pair of rabbis from the Beit Din to make eiruvei tavshilin on their behalf, by way of agency, taking bread and a cooked dish from each house and reciting the formula on their behalf. And if the person knows how to recite the blessing but only does not know the text of the eiruv, the ruling (drawing on a parallel from the laws of Chanukah, where the sick person blesses and another lights on his behalf) is that the head of the household himself recites the blessing, and his agent standing beside him immediately recites the text of the eiruv.
takeaways: One who does not know the text of the eiruv - an agent performs it on his behalf, by way of agency
One who knows how to recite the blessing recites it himself, and the agent recites the text

paragraphs: One must prepare the needs of Shabbat while it is still day, so that there remains time in the day such that, had guests who had not yet eaten happened to arrive, they could eat and enjoy, that same day before twilight, from the work he had done – as our teacher Rabbeinu Zalman, of blessed memory, wrote in the Shulchan Aruch.

clarification.explanation: One must prepare the needs of Shabbat while it is still day, so that there remains enough time in the day that, had guests who had not eaten happened to arrive, they could eat and enjoy from the work done, that same day before twilight. This is a condition of eiruv tavshilin - that the work be done while there is still ample daylight remaining.
takeaways: The needs of Shabbat are prepared while there is still ample daylight remaining, so there would be time for guests to benefit from them that same day
